intro:
This track follows one payment as it leaves a program: from the objects in the program's memory, to bytes on a disk or a network, into a database that outlives the code that wrote it, across a call to another program, and through an order of several steps that must survive a crash. Lessons start from scenes everyone knows, such as a bakery's refund that can't find its payment, a paper order form that gains a new box, a Pay button that asks you not to press it twice, and an online order stuck on Processing. Then they open up the machinery, one byte or one step at a time.

By the end, you can:

- turn a record into bytes in several formats, say what each costs in size and in risk, and spot the one that runs a stranger's code;
- change the shape of a record without breaking the programs that read it, and say which programs must be updated first;
- run two versions of a program against one database, and change a live table in safe steps;
- call another program with a deadline, and retry without charging a card twice;
- write a workflow that carries an order on after a crash, and after a change to its code.

The five lessons:

1. From objects to bytes: JSON, binary formats and serializers
2. Schemas that evolve: Protobuf, Avro and compatibility
3. Data outlives code: rolling upgrades and migrations
4. Calling other services: REST, RPC and gRPC
5. Durable execution: workflows that survive crashes

You need to read a little Kotlin, and to have JDK 21 or newer, the Java toolkit the labs run on. You don't need to know any of the formats or products first: every term is explained the first time it appears. The labs live in one Gradle project, `flow` (Gradle is the tool that builds the labs and runs their tests). From the `labs` folder, run `./gradlew :flow:test --tests 'sfz.enc.lNN.*'` until it passes; `./gradlew :flow:solutionTest` runs the same tests against the finished answers. No code generators are needed: Protobuf is written by hand, gRPC's methods are described in Kotlin, and Temporal runs in its test server inside the program. Only lesson 3 needs Docker, a free program that runs small, separate Linux systems on your laptop, for a PostgreSQL 18 database. The Networking track's lessons on HTTP and on production networking, and the Caching track's lesson on idempotency keys, come back in lessons 4 and 5.
cheatsheet:
## From objects to bytes (lesson 1)

An object in memory points at other objects by address, and an address means nothing outside the program that holds it. So data that is stored or sent is first encoded: turned into self-contained bytes.

| Encoding | The sample payment | Field names in the bytes | Watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| JSON (text) | 116 bytes | yes | many readers keep numbers as doubles, so whole numbers above 2^53 change without an error: send 64-bit IDs as strings; raw bytes need Base64 (+33%) |
| MessagePack, CBOR (binary JSON) | 84, 85 bytes | yes | smaller values, the same names; 39 bytes as a bare list of values |
| BSON | bigger than JSON | yes | adds lengths and type bytes, so a database can skip through it |
| Java serialization | | class names | the bytes choose which classes are created, and run their `readObject`: never use it on bytes from outside; a JEP 290 filter (`maxdepth=5;com.acme.Order;!*`) lists what's allowed |
| Protobuf | 42 bytes | field numbers | never change or reuse a number; mark deleted ones `reserved` |
| Avro | 38 bytes | nothing | the reader needs the writer's exact schema |

## Schemas that evolve (lessons 2 and 3)

- A schema is the agreed shape of a record. **Backward** compatible: new code reads old data. **Forward** compatible: old code reads new data. A rolling upgrade, which replaces a program's copies one at a time, needs both, because for a while both versions read and write the same data.
- Protobuf writes a key per field, `(fieldNumber shl 3) or wireType`, then the value. Varints use 7 bits per byte, lowest bits first; `-1` as `int64` takes 10 bytes, as `sint64` 1. Old code skips unknown fields and keeps them; missing fields read as defaults.
- Avro matches the writer's schema to the reader's by field name. Add or remove only fields that have defaults.
- A schema registry checks each new schema before you deploy. BACKWARD mode (the default) means consumers, the programs that read, upgrade first; FORWARD means producers, the programs that write, upgrade first; FULL checks both. Modes without `_TRANSITIVE` compare only with the latest version, so use the transitive ones while old data is kept.
- Old code that decodes into its own class and writes the class back deletes fields it doesn't know. Change only what you own, or keep unknown fields.
- Never give an old name or number (a field number, a flag, a column) a new meaning: Knight Capital lost over $460 million in 45 minutes that way.
- Expand and contract: add the new shape, write both, copy old rows over (backfill), switch reads, switch writes, and drop the old shape after the last old copy of the program is gone. Set `lock_timeout` before changing a busy table's schema.

## Calling other services (lesson 4)

| | REST | gRPC |
|---|---|---|
| Contract | an OpenAPI 3.2 file (YAML or JSON) | a `.proto` file, with generated client and server code |
| On the wire | resource URLs, HTTP methods, JSON bodies | HTTP/2 POST to `/package.Service/Method`; a 5-byte prefix and Protobuf bytes per message |
| Outcome | HTTP status code | `grpc-status` in the trailers (the HTTP status is 200) |
| Deadline | no standard; each side sets its own timeouts | `grpc-timeout`, sent as time remaining and passed on to later calls (grpc-java, Go) |
| Streaming | no (apart from add-ons) | one request and one reply, or streams in either direction or both |
| Browsers | yes | through gRPC-Web or Connect |

- A remote call can end with no answer, and the client can't tell a lost request from a lost reply. Give every call a deadline: gRPC has none unless you set one.
- Retry `UNAVAILABLE` and, with a key, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`; never `INVALID_ARGUMENT` or `FAILED_PRECONDITION`. Wait a random, growing time between attempts (full jitter), cap the attempts, and retry at one layer only. gRPC's own retry policy retries inside the call's original deadline.
- Idempotency key: one per operation, made before the first attempt, sent with every attempt, claimed by the server in one atomic step before the work, and passed on to the next program down. Stripe: up to 255 characters; the first result is saved once the work begins (even a 500 error); keys may be deleted after 24 hours; the same key with different details is an error; POST only.
- Servers update first, so requests need backward and replies forward compatibility. Stripe pins each account to a dated version and converts replies back; since `2024-09-30.acacia`, a release with no breaking changes every month, and two breaking releases a year.
- One gRPC channel is one HTTP/2 connection. An L4 balancer, which picks a copy per connection, sends all of the channel's calls to one copy. Fix: an L7 proxy that balances each request (Envoy, a service mesh), the client's own `round_robin` over every copy's address, or `maxConnectionAge` as a quick patch.

## Durable execution (lesson 5)

- Workflow: the code that decides the steps; it must be deterministic. Activity: a step that touches the outside world, run at least once and retried (Temporal's default: from 1 s, doubling to 100 s, with no limit on attempts).
- The server keeps an event history for every run, only ever added to. After a crash, a worker replays the workflow code: recorded steps return their saved results, and the first unrecorded step runs for real. `Workflow.sleep` is a timer kept by the server.
- "Exactly once" means progress recorded once. Pass every outside call a key built from the workflow ID and the step: `"$workflowId/charge"`.
- Saga: each step has a compensating step; when a step fails for good, compensate the finished steps, newest first. Others can see the state in between. Put what can't be undone last.
- Never in workflow code: `Random`, `UUID.randomUUID()`, the clock, `Thread.sleep`, threads, files or network calls. Use `Workflow.randomUUID()`, `Workflow.currentTimeMillis()`, `Workflow.sleep()` and activities.
- Changing code while runs are in progress: `Workflow.getVersion(changeId, Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION, 1)` (old histories get -1), or Worker Versioning to keep each run on the version it started on. Replay saved histories with `WorkflowReplayer` before you deploy. A mismatch raises `NonDeterministicException`, which fails the workflow task, and Temporal retries it.
- Kotlin 2.4 with Temporal's Java library 1.40: don't pass method references (`activities::charge`) to `Async` or `Saga`; call activities directly, or pass a lambda.
- Limits: 51,200 events or 50 MB per history, with warnings from 10,240 events or 10 MB; long loops use continue-as-new.
- The workflow ID doubles as a duplicate check for starts; `REJECT_DUPLICATE` keeps it taken after the run closes.

| Engine (November 2026) | Progress is written to | Resumes by |
|---|---|---|
| Temporal (server 1.32, Java library 1.40) | an event history in the Temporal server | replaying the workflow code |
| Restate 1.8 | a journal for each call, in the Restate server | replaying the function |
| DBOS Transact Java 1.2 | rows of saved progress in your own PostgreSQL | running the workflow again with saved step results |
| AWS Step Functions, Standard | the history of each run | moving to the next step (exactly once unless `Retry` is set) |
| AWS Lambda durable functions | checkpoints written by its library | running the function again, skipping saved steps |
recap: Objects point at each other by memory address, which means nothing outside their program, so data that is stored or sent must become self-contained bytes. Java's built-in encoding lets the bytes choose which classes to create and runs their code, so never use it on bytes from outside.

JSON goes everywhere, but many readers turn whole numbers above 2^53 into a nearby value, it has no type for raw bytes, and it writes every field name in every record. Binary JSON shrinks the values and keeps the names.

Protobuf tags each field with a number, so old readers skip fields they don't know and missing ones read as defaults; never reuse a number. Avro writes only values, and matches the writer's schema to the reader's by field name.
Backward compatibility lets new code read old data, and forward compatibility lets old code read new data. A rolling upgrade needs both, and a schema registry checks them before you deploy.
Data outlives code: change a live schema in steps with expand and contract, and never let old code write back fields it doesn't understand.
A call to another program can end with no answer. Give every call a deadline, retry only what didn't get through or is unknown, and only with an idempotency key made once per operation.
REST with OpenAPI and gRPC with Protobuf are two ways to write the contract down. gRPC's one long-lived connection needs balancing per request, in an L7 proxy or in the client.
Durable execution writes down each step's result and replays the code after a crash. Activities still run at least once, so every outside call carries a key built from the workflow ID and the step.
Workflow code must replay the same way every time: change it with `Workflow.getVersion` or pinned versions, and test it against real histories with `WorkflowReplayer`.

quiz.q: A web page reads a payment number, `1849204436731904017`, from a JSON reply with JavaScript's `JSON.parse`. What does it get?
options: The exact number, because JSON numbers are 64-bit
An error, because the number is too large
A nearby number, which can match a different payment
The number as a string, because the reader notices the overflow
quiz.why: `JSON.parse` keeps numbers as doubles, which hold whole numbers exactly only up to 2^53. Bigger ones change silently to a nearby value. The fix from lesson 1 is to send 64-bit numbers as strings.

quiz.q: A program reads bytes from a queue with Java's `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` and casts the result to `Order` on the next line. Why is that dangerous if the bytes come from outside?
options: The cast is slow for large objects
The bytes choose which classes are created, and their `readObject` code runs before your cast
Java serialization can't handle objects inside objects
The cast fails for every class that isn't `Order`, so the program crashes
quiz.why: Reading creates whatever classes the bytes name, and runs their code first. A chain of ordinary classes already in the program, called a gadget chain, can end with an attacker's command running. The `ClassCastException` comes too late. A JEP 290 filter rejects classes before they exist.

quiz.q: A Protobuf field `int64 tip_cents = 7;` was deleted last year. A developer adds `int64 loyalty_points = 7;`. Old records still sit in the database. What happens when new code reads them?
options: Old tips are read as loyalty points, without any error
The reader rejects the old records
Field 7 reads as 0, because the old field was deleted
Protobuf notices that the field's name changed and skips it
quiz.why: The bytes carry only the field number and the wire type, and both match, so the old value lands in the new field. Nothing fails. That's why a deleted number goes into `reserved 7;`, so the compiler refuses to reuse it.

quiz.q: Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs to read, stores Avro records in a topic whose schema a registry checks in BACKWARD mode. You register a compatible new schema. In which order do you deploy?
options: Producers (the writers) first, then consumers (the readers)
All at once, in one release
It doesn't matter, because the registry converts old data
Consumers (the readers) first, then producers (the writers)
quiz.why: BACKWARD means the new schema can read data written with the old one, so the readers must have it before any writer starts using it. FORWARD is the writers-first mode. The registry checks schemas; it converts nothing.

quiz.q: During a rolling upgrade, v1 and v2 of a program share a table. v2 adds a `loyaltyTier` property to a JSON column. A v1 copy reads such a row into its data class (ignoring properties it doesn't know), changes the amount and writes the whole object back. What happens?
options: The write fails, because the JSON no longer matches
`loyaltyTier` is deleted from that row
`loyaltyTier` is kept, because JSON columns keep unknown keys
v1 copies `loyaltyTier` but sets it to null
quiz.why: v1's class has no place for the property, so it never reaches the object, and writing the whole object back drops it. This is the forward-compatibility trap of lesson 3: old code must change only what it owns, or keep the fields it doesn't know.

quiz.q: You must rename the column `email` to `email_address` on a busy table while old code is still running. Which plan never breaks a running version?
options: `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` during a quiet hour
Deploy the new code first, then rename the column
Add `email_address`, write both, copy old rows over, switch reads, switch writes, and drop `email` only after the last old copy is gone
Copy the table, rename the column in the copy and swap the tables
quiz.why: Expand and contract keeps every step compatible with the versions running on both sides of it. A rename breaks whichever version still uses the old name, at any hour. Copying and swapping loses the writes made during the copy.

quiz.q: A gRPC client sends 1,000 calls a second over one channel to a service with 5 copies behind an L4 load balancer. One copy is busy and four are idle. Why?
options: The channel's one HTTP/2 connection was balanced once, when it opened, so every call goes to the same copy
gRPC always sends to the first address that DNS returns
The other four copies failed their health checks
The balancer spreads calls one by one, but the copies have different CPU limits
quiz.why: An L4 balancer picks a copy when a TCP connection opens, and a gRPC channel sends all its calls over one long-lived connection. Balance each request with an L7 proxy, or in the client with `round_robin` over every copy's address.

quiz.q: Which retry setup can't charge a card twice when replies are lost?
options: Retry `POST /charges` up to 3 times with growing waits
Retry with a fresh UUID as the idempotency key on each attempt
Turn on gRPC's retry policy for `UNAVAILABLE`
Make one key per payment before the first attempt, send it with every attempt, and have the server claim it before charging
quiz.why: Only a key that stays the same across attempts lets the server recognize a retry, and claiming it before the work stops two attempts running at once from both charging. The first three options all resend a request that the server can't tell apart from a new payment.

quiz.q: A Temporal worker dies after an order's `charge` and `reserve` activities have finished. Another worker picks the order up. What happens at `charge`?
options: The library returns the charge ID recorded in the event history; the bank isn't called
The library calls the bank again, and the key makes it harmless
The new worker skips the workflow code and starts at the next activity
The workflow starts over as a new run
quiz.why: Replay runs the workflow code from the top, and every activity call whose result is in the history returns that result at once. Keys matter at a different moment: an activity that did its work but never reported back is run again.

quiz.q: A workflow has 40,000 runs asleep in a 24-hour wait, and needs a new activity before `charge`. Which deploy is safe for the sleeping runs?
options: Add the call and deploy; replay skips activities it doesn't recognize
Add the call behind `Workflow.getVersion`, or keep the old runs on the old code with Worker Versioning
Add the call and start every sleeping run again from the beginning
Rename the activity so the history doesn't match it
quiz.why: Replay must send the same commands as the history. `getVersion` returns `DEFAULT_VERSION` for histories recorded before the change, so old runs take the old path; Worker Versioning avoids replaying old runs on new code at all. Deploying the change bare raises `NonDeterministicException` and leaves the runs stuck.
